blocks.text: The name and origin of bees. How they are read to have been found in the lion's carcass. That they hear, are frightened by the ringing of brass, are driven out by smoke, and are remarkable for their bravery, on various passages of Scripture.

The Hebrew דבר means not only to speak but also to order, to rule, to lead, to lead down, following the usage of the Chaldeans. For examples see 1 Sam. VIII, 21. Psal. XLVII, 4. and XVIII, 48. Hence the bee is called in Hebrew דברה debora, in Chaldee דברא dabbara, from its wonderful guidance and order; just as in Arabic دبر [dbr] dabron is a swarm of bees ^{(1)}. For this little creature is a political one, having kings, peoples, [III, 353] cities and palaces. On these, among the Greeks, the chief authorities to consult are Aristotle, Aelian and the writers of the Geoponica; among the Romans, Varro, Virgil, Columella, Pliny; and among the Arabs, Damir and Alkazuinius. I have no leisure to plunder their book-chests on so well-worn a subject.

That bees are generated not only from bees but also from an ox is a constant report among writers. Antigonus, Account of Marvels 23: Ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ τὸν βοῦν ἐὰν κατορύξῃς ἐν τόποις τισὶν, ὥστε αὐτὰ τὰ κέρατα τῆς γῆς ὑπερέχειν, εἶθ᾽ ὕστερον ἀποπρίσῃς, λέγουσιν μελίττας ἐκπέτεσθαι· σαπέντα γὰρ αὐτὸν εἰς τοῦτο διαλύεσθαι τὸ ζῶον [En Aigyptō ton boun ean katoryxēs en topois tisin, hōste auta ta kerata tēs gēs hyperechein, eith᾽ hysteron apopris ēs, legousin melittas ekpetesthai; sapenta gar auton eis touto dialyesthai to zōon]. In some places of Egypt, if you bury an ox so that the horns stand above the ground, and then saw them off, they say that bees fly out; for it, when putrefied, is changed into this animal. Varro likewise on the ox, On Agriculture book 2, chapter 5: I know that from it, when putrefied, are born the sweetest [col. 503] bees, the mothers of honey; from which the Greeks call them βουγόνας [bougonas]. And book 3, chapter 16: Bees are born partly from bees, partly from the putrefied body of an ox. Columella, book 1, chapter 4: That bees can be generated from a slain bullock, Democritus and Mago, and no less Virgil, have reported. Mago indeed affirms that the same happens also from the bellies of oxen. Philo, On Those Who Sacrifice: Μέλιττα ζῶόν ἐστιν οὐ καθαρὸν, ἐκ σήψεως καὶ φθορᾶς νεκρῶν, ὡς ὁ λόγος, βοῶν γεννώμενον [Melitta zōon estin ou katharon, ek sēpseōs kai phthoras nekrōn, hōs ho logos, boōn gennōmenon]; The bee is an impure animal, which they say is born from the putrefaction and corruption of dead oxen. Pliny, book 11, chapter 20: There are some who (think) that bees wholly lost are restored by fresh ox bellies covered with dung. Plutarch at the end of the Cleomenes: Μελίττας μὲν βόες, σφῆκας δὲ ἵπποι κατασαπέντες ἐξανθοῦσι [Melittas men boes, sphēkas de hippoi katasapentes exanthousi]; Putrefied oxen put forth bees, and horses wasps. Aelian at the end of book 2: Ἀποθανὼν δὲ βοῦς γενναῖόν τι χρῆμα, καὶ ἀξιέπαινον· μέλιτται γοῦν ἐκ τῶν ἐκείνου λειψάνων ἐκφύονται [Apothanōn de bous gennaion ti chrēma, kai axiepainon; melittai goun ek tōn ekeinou leipsanōn ekphyontai]. Even a dead ox is an excellent thing and to be highly valued, since bees spring from its remains. Galen, in the book Whether What Is Contained in the Womb Is an Animal, chapter 5: Οὐ δὲ γὰρ ὅπως ἐν φυτοῖς σκώληκες γίνονται, ἢ ἀφ᾽ ἵππων καὶ βοῶν οἱ σφῆκες, καὶ μέλιτται, ῥᾴδιον ἡμῖν λέγειν [Ou de gar hopōs en phytois skōlēkes ginontai, ē aph᾽ hippōn kai boōn hoi sphēkes, kai melittai, rhadion hēmin legein]; For neither is it easy for you to say how worms are generated in plants, or wasps and bees from horses and oxen. Origen, Against Celsus [III, 354] book 4: Since we do not marvel that even now a serpent comes from a dead man, from the marrow of the spine, as they say; and a bee from an ox, a wasp from a horse, a beetle from an ass. Servius on book 4 of the Georgics: There are many kinds of bees. Properly, however, those from oxen are called bees, from horses drones, from mules hornets, from asses wasps. And in what way this happens is related at length by Florentinus in book 15 of the Geoponica, chapter [2], Περὶ μελισσῶν, καὶ πῶς ἂν ἐκ βοὸς γένηται ὃ καλεῖται βουγόνη [Peri melissōn, kai pōs an ek boos genētai ho kaleitai bougonē], On bees, and how what is called BUGONE comes from an ox. Many poets agree, as among the Greeks Philetas in Antigonus: the one, namely, whom Suidas attests was the tutor of Ptolemy II and wrote Elegies and Epigrams.
Βουγενέας φάμενος προσεβήσαο μακρὰ μελίσσας, [Bougeneas phamenos prosebēsao makra melissas,] Having spoken thus, you approached from afar the ox-born bees.
And Archelaus in Varro, when he calls bees
— — βοὸς φθιμένης πεποιημένα τέκνα, [boos phthimenēs pepoiēmena tekna,]
the manufactured offspring of a corrupted cow. And the same again,
Ἵππων μὲν σφῆκες γενεαὶ, μόσχων δὲ μέλισσαι· [Hippōn men sphēkes geneai, moschōn de melissai;] Wasps born from horses, but bees from the origin of bulls.
Whom Nicander imitates thus in the Theriaca, line 741.
Ἵπποι γὰρ σφηκῶν γένεσις, ταῦροι δὲ μελισσῶν, Σκήνεσι πυθομένοισι, λυκοσπάδες ἐξεγένοντο· [Hippoi gar sphēkōn genesis, tauroi de melissōn, Skēnesi pythomenoisi, lykospades exegenonto;]

For horses torn by wolves generated wasps, and bulls bees, from their corrupted bodies. (Note in passing that σκῆνος [skēnos], tent, is taken for body, as by Paul 2 Cor. V, 1. 4.). And Ovid in book 15 of the Metamorphoses,
